# Neumann — The Origins and History of Consciousness (1954)

## Bibliographic identity

Erich Neumann's *The Origins and History of Consciousness*, translated from the German by R. F. C. Hull, was first published in English by Princeton University Press in 1954 (Bollingen Series XLV); the German original, *Ursprungsgeschichte des Bewusstseins*, appeared in 1949.

**Consulted edition (in hand, 2026-08-05):** the Princeton Classics reissue, Princeton University Press, 2014, paperback, ISBN 978-0-691-16359-8. This is the same Hull translation and retains Jung's foreword. It is a direct reissue of the 1954 Bollingen text; pagination is assumed to reproduce the 1954 layout, but that equivalence must be confirmed against the physical copy before page-located citation. The publisher record (press.princeton.edu) corroborates edition, series, translation, and foreword; the 1954 first-edition record is corroborated by Open Library and national-library catalogue data (accessed 2026-07-16).

## Source scholarship

Neumann's work is the post-Jungian historical morphology of ego formation: a phylogenetic account in which the individual ego's development recapitulates the history of consciousness as it is carried in myth. The mythic sequence — uroboros → Great Mother → separation of the world parents → birth of the hero → slaying of the mother → slaying of the father → transformation → liberation of the captive — is read as the progressive differentiation of ego-consciousness from the maternal-unconscious ground. Part II maps the same sequence onto the historical stages of ego-consciousness proper.

Relevant operations for this essay:

- **The uroboros** — the self-containing round, the pre-egoic psychic whole that holds both parents in one figure; the psyche's own image of the undifferentiated condition before the cut.
- **The Great Mother** — the maternal uroboros as the first object-face of the unconscious; the archetype's split into good/bad mother.
- **The separation of the world parents** — the first differentiation of the primordial couple (Father Heaven / Mother Earth); the principle of opposites born from the one round. The split of the archetype into good and evil figures (the two parents, the twins) belongs to this same movement.
- **The hero** — the evolving ego-consciousness; the hero's slayings (of the mother, of the father) are the ego's achieved differentiations, and his descent/return is the relation back through the ground it left.
- **The transformation stage** — consciousness opening beyond the ego-hero toward the transpersonal; the inner counterpart of the ego's outward victories.
- **The ascent of consciousness and the species-name (p. 16, lead)** — consciousness as the "unnatural" thing in nature, specific to the species that "has justly styled himself Homo sapiens"; the struggle between the specifically human and the universally natural constitutes the history of conscious development. Transcription pending collation against the physical 2014 copy. The word-field this passage opens (homo/humus, sapiens/sapientia) is the project's own reading, carried in the earth/taste/wisdom etymology history; it is not Neumann's claim.

Neighbouring series: Neumann's stadial morphology and Gebser's structures of consciousness (archaic → magical → mythical → mental → integral) are both phylogenetic, structural accounts of consciousness; their methods, periodisations, and objects differ, and any relation drawn between them must be an operational homology, not an identification. Neumann's status here is the mythic-historical psychology that the essay's topological-mathematical claim does not derive from.

No passage is quotation-ready. These are collation targets for Frank's reading of the 2014 copy; chapter titles and page ranges must be confirmed against the physical book.

- Part I ch. I, The Uroboros — the self-containing round; uroboros with phallus; the round as both-parents-in-one.
- Part I ch. I region, p. 16 — "The ascent toward consciousness is the 'unnatural' thing in nature; it is specific to the species of Man, who on that account has justly styled himself Homo sapiens. The struggle between the specifically human and the universally natural constitutes the historically human and the universally natural constitutes the history of man's conscious development." **Collation note:** the NOTES transcription doubles a clause; the published sentence appears to run "…constitutes the history of man's conscious development." Verify exact wording, punctuation, and section heading against the 2014 copy before promotion.
- Part I ch. II, The Great Mother — maternal uroboros; the split of the mother archetype into good/bad.
- Part I ch. III, The Separation of the World Parents: The Principle of Opposites — the first differentiation; opposites born from the one round.
- Part I, hero division ch. I, The Birth of the Hero — ego-consciousness as hero; the dragon/boundary slayings.
- Part I, hero division ch. II, The Slaying of the Mother — the ego's first great differentiation from the maternal ground.
- Part I, hero division ch. III, The Slaying of the Father — the ego's separation from the paternal principle; the fathers' two forms (good/evil, heavenly/tyrannical).
- Part I, transformation division ch. I (pp. 195–219 in the publisher-hosted contents) — the captive/treasure movement; exact selected-copy passages remain to be collated.
- Part I, transformation division ch. II (pp. 220–256 in that contents) — Osiris and transformation; the transpersonal turn. The earlier consecutive VII/VIII labels and ordering were inaccurate.
- Part II — the historical stages of ego-consciousness; the recapitulation thesis (exact chapter titles to be collated against the physical copy).

## Navigation verification — 2026-09-08

The [publisher-hosted JSTOR contents](https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctvx5wbkw) confirms separate creation, hero and transformation divisions in Part I, with chapter numbering restarting in each. The first division spans chapters I–III (pp. 5–38, 39–101, 102–128); the hero division I–III spans pp. 131–151, 152–169, 170–192; the transformation division I–II spans pp. 195–219, 220–256. Part II has four lettered divisions spanning pp. 259–312, 313–360, 361–394 and 395–418. These are verified electronic navigation ranges, not a claim that Frank's 2014 physical-copy pagination has been collated. Full chapter retrieval was unavailable this run. No NOTES quotation has been promoted; `quote_status: no-excerpts` remains.
